@@ -0,0 +1,56 @@
+# Plan: Active-subspace reparameterization of rainfall-runoff calibration
+
+## Option being planned
+
+"Reparameterize the calibration with active subspaces to shorten the MCMC chain" — identify the few data-informed directions along which the negative log-likelihood varies (the active subspace), run Metropolis-Hastings only on those, and draw the inactive directions independently from the prior [s1]. The question this plan answers: **does the four-parameter GR4J calibration posterior admit a low-dimensional active subspace, and does running MCMC only on it beat both a serial chain and side-by-side chains — and is that verdict itself changed by buying more parallel compute?**
+
+## What to build
+
+1. **Differentiable GR4J forward model in JAX.** GR4J has exactly four calibrated parameters — production-store capacity X1 (mm), groundwater exchange X2 (mm/day), routing-store capacity X3 (mm), unit-hydrograph time base X4 (days) [s10]. Implement the webGR equations (production store, percolation, two unit hydrographs, routing store, groundwater exchange) so that the negative log-likelihood is differentiable w.r.t. all four parameters by automatic differentiation. This gives one forward **plus one adjoint pass** per gradient sample (or two forward evaluations by finite difference) [s7].
+2. **Active-subspace estimator.** Draw M independent prior samples; for each compute the misfit gradient ∇f; average the outer products into the matrix Ĉ = (1/M) Σ ∇fᵢ∇fᵢᵀ; eigendecompose. Report the eigenvalue spectrum λ1..λ4 and the spectral gap. This is the standard Monte Carlo estimator [s8].
+3. **Active-subspace MCMC.** Metropolis-Hastings on the n active variables (n = 1 or 2, chosen by the eigenvalue gap), with the per-step approximate likelihood ĝ(y) = (1/Mg) Σ f(W1·y + W2·zᵢ) using Mg = 10 conditional-average samples, and P = 10 independent prior draws on the inactive variables per reconstructed parameter [s1, s14]. Reconstruct the 4-D chain x = W1·y + W2·z.
+4. **Two baselines.** (a) *serial*: JAX-compiled random-walk Metropolis on all four parameters, proposal variance tuned to ~25% acceptance, 500,000 forward evaluations (the same budget the published comparison used) [s4]. (b) *copies*: independent vanilla chains started from dispersed points, one per GPU, run side by side.
+5. **Metric.** Minimum effective sample size (ESS) per component via the autocorrelation sum N/(1+2Σρₖ), exactly the published definition [s5], reported per forward evaluation and per wall-clock hour.
+
+## Baseline
+
+Vanilla random-walk Metropolis on all four GR4J parameters at 500,000 forward evaluations. In the published 100-parameter analogue this baseline reaches a minimum ESS of 604 while the active-subspace-accelerated chain reaches 81,986 at the same evaluation budget [s5]. The GR4J comparison reuses the identical budget and definition; the only differences are the 4-parameter forward model and the artificial bimodality that cheap fixed-step integration is known to inject [s9].
+
+## How to check it is right
+
+1. **Anchor — reproduce the published two-parameter quadratic.** Forward model m(x) = ½·xᵀAx with A = Q·diag(1, ε)·Qᵀ, Q = ½[[√2,√2],[−√2,√2]], noise σ² = 0.1, data d = 0.9 [s1]. With ε = 0.01 the paper reports "the gap between the eigenvalues suggests an active one-dimensional active subspace" [s6]; with ε = 0.95 there is no gap. My estimator must recover λ1/λ2 ≳ 100 at ε = 0.01 and λ1/λ2 ≲ 10 at ε = 0.95, matching the published scripts (bitbucket.org/paulcon/accelerating-mcmc-with-active-subspaces). Failing this stops the spend.
+2. **Forward-model check.** The JAX GR4J must reproduce the webGR equations verbatim and match the airGR reference on a fixed parameter set.
+3. **ESS magnitude check.** The accelerated chain's min-ESS jump must reproduce the published 604 → 81,986 magnitude [s5] before I trust the GR4J result.
+4. **Bias check.** The accelerated chain's posterior mean and covariance must match a long serial reference chain within a stated tolerance (the Hellinger-distance bound the paper derives [s1]).
+
+## The compute question (what the money actually tests)
+
+The pipeline is four serial steps: draw M gradient samples → average outer products → eigendecompose → run the active-variable chain. The M gradient samples are mutually independent, so they run concurrently across GPUs; only the eigendecomposition and the short low-dimensional chain stay serial. The quantity more parallel compute buys is therefore **M, the number of gradient samples**. The published demos stop at M = 300 (one-dimensional subspace) [s8] and M = 1000 (100-parameter model, two-dimensional subspace) [s3]. The plan sweeps M ∈ {100, 300, 1000, 10000, 100000} on GR4J and asks whether the eigenvalue gap and the accelerated-chain ESS verdict change with M:
+
+- **if_lever**: more samples make the gap appear/widen, so the accelerated chain only beats both baselines at high M.
+- **if_not**: the gap is already clear at M = 300, so 100× more samples change nothing — compute is not the lever, the reparameterization is.
+
+Decision rule: compute is the lever only if λ1/λ2 at 100,000 samples is ≥ 2× that at 300, or the accelerated chain's min-ESS at 100,000 is ≥ 2× that at 300; otherwise compute is not the lever. Noise rule: 10 independent prior-sample batches for bootstrap spectral ranges, 3 seeds per MCMC run, differences declared only on non-overlapping ranges.
+
+## Cost
+
+Rates (Lambda on-demand, read 2026-10-20): 1× NVIDIA A6000 (48 GB) at $1.09/GPU/hr [s12]; 8× NVIDIA A100 SXM (80 GB) at $2.79/GPU/hr [s13]. Filesystem ~$0.20/GiB-month.
+
+| line | phase | instance | hours | cost |
+|---|---|---|---|---|
+| pilot: JAX GR4J + 1000-sample spectral estimate, time it | pilot | 1×A6000 | 2 h (need ≈ 0.5 h) | $2.18 |
+| reproduce: two-parameter anchor + ESS comparison | reproduce | 1×A6000 | 2 h (need ≈ 0.5 h) | $2.18 |
+| spectrum sweep M∈{100…100000} | spectrum_sweep | 1×A6000 | 2 h (need ≈ 0.2 h) | $2.18 |
+| three arms at 500k evaluations | mcmc_compare | 1×A6000 | 4 h (need ≈ 1 h) | $4.36 |
+| optional: 671-catchment CAMELS sweep | camels | 8×A100 | 2 h (need ≈ 0.6 h) | $44.64 |
+| storage (CAMELS forcing + results, 5 GiB) | camels | — | — | $1.00 |
+
+**Total ≈ $56.54, hard stop $200.** The fact that this sits ~$57 under the $1000 ceiling is itself the answer to the root question: for a four-parameter lumped model the active-subspace computation is not compute-bound. The only line that meaningfully uses parallel GPUs is the 671-catchment sweep, and even that is minutes of GPU time.
+
+## What $1000 cannot buy here
+
+The genuinely compute-bound extension — active-subspace reparameterization of a hundreds-of-parameter distributed model (the high-performance-computing regime the framer names) across all catchments — is out of scope at any price near this budget and is left open.
+
+## Human time / outside budget
+
+~8 hours of my time writing and debugging the JAX pipeline; CAMELS download (a few GiB, free).

@@ -0,0 +1,120 @@
+"""Pilot: GR4J forward + batched multi-chain Metropolis throughput.
+
+Run under `timeout 300` on the local 4-core CPU (dev), then on the A6000
+(Lambda, JAX CUDA backend) to measure `batched_forward_ms` and
+`cpu_671_hours`. This is the script referenced by phase gpu_bench.
+
+Not run here (no exec in this environment): numbers that depend on its output
+are basis GUESS with measured_by=gpu_bench.
+"""
+import time
+import numpy as np
+
+try:
+    import jax
+    import jax.numpy as jnp
+    HAS_JAX = True
+except Exception:
+    HAS_JAX = False
+
+
+def gr4j_scan(params, precip, pet):
+    """Vectorized GR4J over a batch of catchments (params: [B,4]).
+    Returns daily streamflow [B,T]. Serial scan over T days; batched over B.
+    Production store (S) and routing store (R) are the only recurrences.
+    Unit hydrographs are applied via convolution over the full series.
+    """
+    B = params.shape[0]
+    T = precip.shape[1]
+    x1 = params[:, 0]
+    x2 = params[:, 1]
+    x3 = params[:, 2]
+    x4 = params[:, 3]
+
+    # UH1 time base x4 days, UH2 time base 2*x4 days (S-curve, standard GR4J)
+    x4b = np.maximum(x4, 0.5)
+    uh1 = _uh_ordinates(x4b)
+    uh2 = _uh_ordinates(2.0 * x4b)
+
+    S = 0.3 * x1          # initial production store
+    R = 0.5 * x3          # initial routing store
+    Pr = np.zeros_like(precip)
+    for t in range(T):
+        P = precip[:, t]
+        E = pet[:, t]
+        Pn = np.maximum(0.0, P - E)
+        En = np.maximum(0.0, E - P)
+        Ps = np.where(
+            Pn > 0,
+            x1 * (1.0 - (S / x1) ** 2) * np.tanh(Pn / x1) / (1.0 + (S / x1) * np.tanh(Pn / x1)),
+            0.0,
+        )
+        Es = np.where(
+            En > 0,
+            S * (2.0 - S / x1) * np.tanh(En / x1) / (1.0 + (1.0 - S / x1) * np.tanh(En / x1)),
+            0.0,
+        )
+        S = S - Es + Ps
+        Perc = S * (1.0 - (1.0 + (4.0 * S / (9.0 * x1)) ** 4.0) ** -0.25)
+        S = S - Perc
+        Pr[:, t] = Perc + Pn - Ps
+
+    Q9 = 0.9 * _conv_series(Pr, uh1) + 0.1 * _conv_series(Pr, uh2)
+    Q = np.zeros_like(precip)
+    for t in range(T):
+        F = x2 * (R / x3) ** 3.5
+        R = np.maximum(0.0, R + Q9[:, t] + F)
+        Qr = R * (1.0 - (1.0 + (R / x3) ** 4.0) ** -0.25)
+        R = R - Qr
+        Qd = np.maximum(0.0, Q9[:, t] + F)
+        Q[:, t] = Qr + Qd
+    return Q
+
+
+def _uh_ordinates(x4):
+    # continuous S-curve unit hydrograph ordinates, max 100 days
+    nh = 100
+    t = np.arange(1, nh + 1).astype(float)
+    sh1 = np.where(t <= 0, 0.0, np.where(t < x4, (t / x4) ** 2.5, 1.0))
+    sh1 = np.where(t <= 0, 0.0, np.where(t < x4, (t / x4) ** 2.5, 1.0))
+    uh = sh1[1:] - sh1[:-1]
+    return uh
+
+
+def _conv_series(pr, uh):
+    B, T = pr.shape
+    out = np.zeros_like(pr)
+    n = min(uh.shape[1] if uh.ndim == 2 else uh.shape[0], T)
+    for k in range(n):
+        w = uh[:, k] if uh.ndim == 2 else uh[k]
+        out[:, k:] += pr[:, : T - k] * w[:, None] if uh.ndim == 2 else pr[:, : T - k] * w
+    return out
+
+
+def main():
+    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
+    B = 2684           # 671 catchments x 4 chains
+    T = 7300           # 20 years daily
+    precip = rng.uniform(0, 50, (B, T))
+    pet = rng.uniform(0, 8, (B, T))
+    params = rng.uniform(1, 1000, (B, 4))
+
+    # warm-up
+    gr4j_scan(params[:8], precip[:8], pet[:8])
+
+    # single forward pass timing (batched over all B)
+    t0 = time.time()
+    gr4j_scan(params, precip, pet)
+    dt_batch = time.time() - t0
+    print(f"batched_forward_ms (B={B}, T={T}) = {dt_batch*1000:.3f}")
+
+    # single-catchment forward pass timing
+    t0 = time.time()
+    for _ in range(10):
+        gr4j_scan(params[:1], precip[:1], pet[:1])
+    dt_one = (time.time() - t0) / 10
+    print(f"single_forward_ms (B=1) = {dt_one*1000:.3f}")
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    main()

+# Plan: Large-sample multi-catchment calibration (CAMELS)
+
+Option: "Large-sample multi-catchment calibration (CAMELS)".
+Root question: what limits Bayesian calibration of rainfall-runoff models (long MCMC chains) — is compute a blocker, and does a shit ton of GPU parallelism fix it?
+
+## What this option claims
+
+CAMELS gives 671 US catchments, each independently calibratable, so the study is embarrassingly parallel. The claim: at CAMELS scale, GPU/cloud throughput directly determines how many catchments get a *proper Bayesian treatment* (MCMC posterior) instead of point optimization. Left open: what extending full Bayesian treatment to all 671 (or globally) would change about large-sample hydrological conclusions.
+
+## What I will build
+
+1. A **GPU-batched GR4J** (4 parameters; Perrin et al. 2003) written in JAX, vectorized over catchments × chains: one forward pass evaluates every chain of every catchment in a single `lax.scan` over the ~7,300-day record. This is the same "many chains on one GPU" pattern shown to scale linearly (ChEES-HMC).
+2. A **multi-chain Metropolis sampler (DREAM(ZS)-style, 4 chains/catchment)** that runs all 2,684 chains side by side, with Gelman–Rubin R̂ as the convergence gate.
+3. A **point-optimization baseline** (airGR `Calibration_Michel` / SCE-UA), the standard large-sample practice.
+4. A **vectorized CPU baseline** (same sampler, JAX CPU backend) so the GPU speedup is measured on the same hardware class.
+
+## The test
+
+Vary the number of catchments given full Bayesian treatment — 67, 335, 671 — and measure wall-clock on one A6000 (1×, $1.09/GPU/hr) versus the vectorized CPU baseline and versus point optimization. The measured outcome is: does GPU throughput decide how many catchments get full Bayesian treatment?
+
+- **if_lever**: one GPU gives ≥20× over CPU and finishes all 671 in < 1 hr, so compute is the lever.
+- **if_not**: a vectorized CPU finishes all 671 in a couple of hours, so throughput does not decide who gets full Bayesian treatment (tradition/software do).
+- **Expected**: if_not — GR4J's forward model is so cheap that full Bayesian over 671 catchments is a small job once vectorized (~10^14 flops total).
+
+## How I check it is right
+
+- Anchor: reproduce airGR's GR4J example — parameter set X=(165.05, 6.46, 422.50, 2.45) gives calibration NSE 0.495 on the L0123001 basin (airGR docs). Match within ±0.02.
+- Independent code: daily flows match airGR `RunModel_GR4J` within 1% mean absolute relative error on 20 random CAMELS catchments.
+- Convergence: R̂ < 1.2 on all 4 parameters before summarizing.
+- Scaling: GPU throughput (chains/s) stays linear from 67 → 335 → 671 catchments.
+
+## Cost (Lambda on-demand, read 2026-10-20)
+
+Rate: NVIDIA A6000 1×, 48 GB, $1.09/GPU/hr (1-GPU table).
+
+| line | phase | kind | hours | need | usd |
+|---|---|---|---|---|---|
+| L_gpu_bench | gpu_bench | work | 2 (time box) | 0.5 | 2.18 |
+| L_main_671 | main_full_bayes | work | 3 (time box) | main_run_hours ≈ 0.22 | 3.27 |
+| L_cpu_baseline | cpu_baseline | work | 1 (time box) | cpu_671_hours ≈ 3 | 1.09 |
+| L_point_opt | baseline_point_opt | work | 1 (time box) | 1 | 1.09 |
+| L_storage | main_full_bayes | storage | — | — | 0.07 |
+| L_stretch_global (optional) | stretch_global | work | 10 (time box) | — | 10.90 |
+
+Core total ≈ **$7.70**; hard stop **$1,000**. The low number is itself the finding: full Bayesian GR4J over 671 catchments is cheap, so compute is probably not the blocker. The optional stretch spends leftover budget on the global CAMELS family (~2,300 catchments) and 3 forcings if the lever shows up.
+
+## Key numbers and bases
+
+- 671 catchments — CITED (Addor et al. 2017, HESS).
+- 20 years of records (≈7,300 days) — CITED (same).
+- 4 GR4J parameters — CITED (INRAE webGR).
+- 4 chains/catchment — DESIGN (within DREAM(ZS)'s cited "N = 3 to 5").

+- cpu_671_hours = 3 — GUESS (measured in gpu_bench).

+- R̂ < 1.2 — CITED (spotpy / Laloy & Vrugt).
+

+

Related problems are counted here as compute constrained in the broad sense: (a) it is still open whether more parallel compute would change the answer, (b) compute is already known to bind there (marked "settled"), or (c) the answer takes long because its steps run one after another even though more hardware would not change the answer, only how soon it arrives.

## Single-chain MCMC mixing

A single Markov chain for a lumped conceptual model must run many serial iterations because posterior samples are autocorrelated; each step conditions on the previous state, and more parallel compute cannot shorten the chain's integrated autocorrelation time, only how fast samples accumulate.

- **root_link:** Bears on the "what actually limits Bayesian calibration" half of the question — the single chain's autocorrelation is why lumped-model calibration is not compute-bound.
- **compute_open:** none — more parallel compute buys samples-per-second but not a shorter autocorrelation time for a single chain, because τ (equivalently ESS = N/(1+2Σρ_k)) is set by target geometry and sampler, not by hardware (https://mc-stan.org/docs/2_31/reference-manual/effective-sample-size.html).
- **sequential:** One converged posterior waits on one chain whose every step is a proposal from the current state plus a Metropolis accept/reject, and a single GR4J forward run is only a few thousand arithmetic steps per multi-decade daily record (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022169403002257), yet the chain must run on the order of up to 10^6 generations (DREAM(D)'s default maximum T_max; https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-15-3701-2011) to overcome autocorrelation, and the answer needs only a few independent chains (DREAM(ZS) uses N = 3–5; https://doi.org/10.1029/2011WR010608) for Gelman–Rubin checks, each keeping a tiny fraction of one GPU busy. These steps must run in order because each state conditions on the previous one, so the only way to run them at the same time is to run many independent chains in parallel, which pays off when the target is multimodal and chains are cheap (it buys coverage, not lower τ) — the nearest source that tried it is DREAM (https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/accelerating-markov-chain-monte-carlo-simulation-by-differential-).
- **sources:** https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022169403002257 · https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-15-3701-2011 · https://mc-stan.org/docs/2_31/reference-manual/effective-sample-size.html

## Ensemble / differential-evolution MCMC

DREAM-style samplers run N chains simultaneously, generating each chain's proposal from differences of other chains' states; this improves exploration of multimodal/correlated hydrologic posteriors and enables Gelman–Rubin cross-chain diagnostics, and it is the one place where more GPUs change what gets sampled (by raising chain count) without lowering per-chain autocorrelation.

- **root_link:** Bears on the "whether a shit ton of GPUs fixes it" half — GPUs buy more parallel chains (throughput and multimodal coverage), a real but bounded fix.
- **compute_open:** More parallel compute buys simultaneous chains (ensemble members); standard DREAM runs N = d/2 to d (up to 2d) chains (https://doi.org/10.1029/2011WR010608), DREAM(ZS) needs only N = 3–5, and the largest reported run uses N = 25 chains on a 25-dimensional trimodal target (https://pure.uva.nl/ws/files/1553085/134391_wrcr13130_sup_0002_t02.txt), but it is still unknown whether chains beyond N = 25 further improve posterior coverage or mixing on higher-dimensional, more multimodal hydrology targets.
- **sequential:** none — after burn-in the N chains' joint density factorizes and they are independent, so the ensemble already splits into N chains run simultaneously (https://doi.org/10.1029/2011WR010608).
- **sources:** https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/accelerating-markov-chain-monte-carlo-simulation-by-differential- · https://doi.org/10.1029/2011WR010608 · https://pure.uva.nl/ws/files/1553085/134391_wrcr13130_sup_0002_t02.txt

## Expensive distributed forward models

For spatially distributed models with hundreds-to-thousands of parameters the forward-model cost dominates the calibration budget, and the workload decomposes into thousands of independent model runs that are embarrassingly parallel across chains and parameter sets; here compute is a genuinely binding constraint that parallelism relieves.

- **root_link:** Bears on the "what actually limits Bayesian calibration" half — for expensive distributed models the forward-model cost, not mixing, is the binding limit.
- **compute_open:** settled: more parallel compute is already known to bind and pay off here — the forward model dominates the budget (DREAM needed about 50 million surrogate-model evaluations to converge on a 241-parameter groundwater model, https://doi.org/10.1029/2011WR010608), distributed MT-DREAM(ZS) reports "spectacular performance improvement" on that same 241-parameter problem (https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2011wr010608), and GPU optimization of the MGB model yields up to 20× CPU speedup for calibration and 24× (CPU) / 65× (GPU) for simulations (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envsoft.2021.105271).
- **sequential:** none — the calibration already decomposes into independent forward-model runs evaluated in parallel across chains and multiple simultaneous proposals, so it is embarrassingly parallel (https://doi.org/10.1029/2011WR010608).
- **sources:** https://doi.org/10.1029/2011WR010608 · https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envsoft.2021.105271 · https://nhess.copernicus.org/articles/12/2411/2012/nhess-12-2411-2012.pdf

## Large-sample multi-catchment calibration

Calibrating many catchments (CAMELS provides 671 US catchments) is embarrassingly parallel because each catchment is independently calibratable, so GPU/cloud throughput directly determines how many catchments get a proper Bayesian treatment rather than point optimization.

- **root_link:** Bears on the "whether a shit ton of GPUs fixes it" half — at CAMELS scale, throughput determines how many catchments can be afforded full Bayesian treatment.
- **compute_open:** More parallel compute buys catchments given full Bayesian treatment instead of point optimization; the largest published set is CAMELS's 671 US catchments (https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/21/5293/2017/hess-21-5293-2017.html), and it is still unknown what extending full Bayesian treatment to all catchments above 671 (or globally) would change about large-sample hydrological conclusions.
- **sequential:** none — the catchments are independently calibratable, so the study already splits into one independent calibration per catchment (https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/21/5293/2017/hess-21-5293-2017.html).
- **sources:** https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/21/5293/2017/hess-21-5293-2017.html · https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hyp.3360060305

3: ## 1. My understanding, relayed before answering
4: 
5: Rainfall-runoff (RR) models map precipitation (and potential evapotranspiration) onto streamflow at a catchment outlet. The workhorse class for calibration studies is the lumped conceptual model — GR4J is the canonical example, with exactly **four** calibrated parameters and a simple production-store + unit-hydrograph structure evaluated a few thousand arithmetic steps per decade of daily data (Perrin, Michel & Andréassian 2003, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022169403002257). Bayesian calibration treats parameters as random and uses Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to sample the posterior p(θ | data).
6: 
7: Two facts dominate this literature:
8: 
9: 1. **Equifinality** — many different parameter sets reproduce the observed hydrograph almost equally well, so the posterior is broad, correlated, and often multimodal rather than a tight Gaussian around a single optimum. Beven & Binley (1992) state it directly: "within the limitations of a given model structure and errors in boundary conditions and field observations, different sets of values may be equally likely as simulators of a catchment" (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hyp.3360060305).
10: 2. **Peculiar response surfaces** — hydrological model parameters are "highly correlated and interdependent," which is precisely what makes naive samplers mix slowly; summarizing/exploring the posterior is the stated bottleneck that "hindered widespread use of Bayesian techniques in hydrology" (Marshall, Nott & Sharma 2004, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2003WR002378). MCMC inefficiency is "frequently caused by an inappropriate selection of the proposal distribution" — a geometric/algorithmic problem, not a hardware one (Vrugt et al. 2009, https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/accelerating-markov-chain-monte-carlo-simulation-by-differential-).
11: 
12: MCMC samples are autocorrelated. The information content of a chain of length N is the effective sample size ESS = N / (1 + 2Σρ_k), where ρ_k are lag autocorrelations; slow mixing inflates the integrated autocorrelation time τ and forces long chains to reach any target ESS (Stan Reference Manual, https://mc-stan.org/docs/2_31/reference-manual/effective-sample-size.html). The integrated autocorrelation time is defined as the number of correlated samples needed, on average, to produce one independent draw (LaplacesDemon IAT/ESS documentation, https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/LaplacesDemon/help/ESS.html). So "needs long MCMC chains" is a symptom of large τ — a statistical property — not directly a statement about hardware speed.
13: 
14: ## 2. Predictions (stated before checking)
15: 
16: - **P1:** For a single lumped conceptual catchment, one forward run is so cheap that the likelihood is effectively free; the binding constraint is τ (mixing), not FLOPs.
17: - **P2:** The "long chains" requirement is a property of posterior geometry (correlation/equifinality/multimodality) and, secondarily, of numerical implementation; it is reduced by better samplers/reparameterizations, not by more cores.
18: - **P3:** GPUs help only where the problem decomposes into independent units of work: many chains (ensemble MCMC), many particles (SMC), many catchments (large-sample), or many forward runs (GLUE / expensive models). They cannot shorten a *single* chain's autocorrelation.
19: - **P4:** There are genuinely compute-bound levels — expensive distributed/high-dimensional models and large-sample (CAMELS-scale) studies — where more parallel compute changes what is even attempted.
20: 
21: ## 3. Analysis
22: 
23: ### 3.1 Why chains are long: geometry and numerics, not throughput
24: 
25: The reason hydrology needed MCMC at all — and found it hard — is that the posterior of a conceptual RR model is difficult to summarize and explore because parameters are strongly correlated (Marshall et al. 2004, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2003WR002378). Equifinality formalizes this as "equal finality": many parameter pathways reproduce the observed runoff (Beven & Binley 1992, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hyp.3360060305). The DREAM paper's motivating diagnosis is that slow mixing "is frequently caused by an inappropriate selection of the proposal distribution," and its remedy is a self-adaptive differential-evolution proposal that tunes scale and orientation during the search — i.e., a better *algorithm*, not more *hardware* (Vrugt et al. 2009, https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/accelerating-markov-chain-monte-carlo-simulation-by-differential-).
26:

That is why "just add GPUs" is not, by itself, a fix for slow mixing — it changes throughput, not τ.
28: 
29: There is also a subtlety specific to hydrology: **cheap numerics corrupt MCMC**. First-order, explicit, fixed-step integration of water-balance dynamics makes the model "computationally cheap" (explicitly desirable for MCMC), but that cheapness introduces artificial bimodality in marginal posteriors and causes "slow convergence of the MCMC algorithm" plus unreliable Gelman–Rubin diagnostics (Schoups et al. 2010, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdfdirect/10.1029/2009WR008648). Here the fix is a better ODE integrator (adaptive-step, second-order, or operator splitting), again not more compute.
30: 
31: ### 3.2 The per-evaluation cost is not the binding constraint (lumped models)

A multi-decade daily simulation is a few thousand arithmetic steps. Tellingly, the original GLUE paper could call its procedure "computationally intensive" only because it ran on a 1992 "local parallel processing computer" (Beven & Binley 1992, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hyp.3360060305) — the same embarrassingly parallel random sampling is trivial on any modern machine. For this model class, the bottleneck is the number of *serial* MCMC iterations needed to overcome τ, not the cost of each iteration.
34: 
35: ### 3.3 What "a shit ton of GPU parallelism" actually buys
36: 
37: MCMC within a single chain is inherently sequential (each state conditions on the previous one), so the only exploitable parallelism is across independent units of work. That covers three regimes:
38: 
39: - **(a) Ensemble / differential-evolution MCMC.** DREAM "runs multiple different chains simultaneously for global exploration" (Vrugt et al. 2009, https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/accelerating-markov-chain-monte-carlo-simulation-by-differential-). Jeremiah et al. note that parallel chains "with different starting points enable the sampler to simultaneously explore multiple regions of the parameter space, thereby improving the posterior coverage over that of a single chain" (https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2010WR010217). GPUs/cloud make thousands of chains cheap, which helps multimodal coverage and yields cross-chain convergence diagnostics — a real, but bounded, improvement (it does not reduce τ).
40: 
41: - **(b) Expensive forward models.** For spatially distributed models with hundreds-to-thousands of parameters, the cost of the forward model dominates, and "high-performance computing"/distributed computing delivers a "spectacular performance improvement" for the MT-DREAM(ZS) sampler on problems up to 241 parameters (Laloy & Vrugt 2012, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2011wr010608). GPU-optimized large-basin models report ~20× CPU speedups for calibration and ~65× GPU speedups for simulations (Freitas et al. 2022, https://experts.illinois.edu/en/publications/performance-optimization-of-the-mgb-hydrological-model-for-multi-). At the SWAT end of the spectrum, calibration "could take days to complete, even on the finest standalone machines" (nhess 2012, https://nhess.copernicus.org/articles/12/2411/2012/nhess-12-2411-2012.pdf). This level is genuinely compute-bound, and parallelism is the fix because calibration decomposes into thousands of independent model runs.
42: 
43: - **(c) Large-sample studies.** CAMELS provides 671 US catchments (Addor et al. 2017, https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/21/5293/2017/hess-21-5293-2017.html), each independently calibratable — the definition of an embarrassingly parallel workload in which GPU/cloud throughput directly determines how many catchments can be afforded a *proper* Bayesian treatment rather than point optimization.
44: 
45: ### 3.4 What compute cannot buy
46: 
47: Three hard limits are not computable away:
48: 
49: 1. **Structural error and input (rainfall) uncertainty.** The model is wrong and the rainfall is mismeasured. Renard et al. (2010) report that "poor identifiability may arise when the inference scheme represents rainfall and structural errors using separate probabilistic models," and emphasize "the inherent limitations of inferring inaccurate hydrologic models using rainfall-runoff data with large unknown errors" (https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2009WR008328). Explicitly accounting for precipitation error "significantly alters the posterior distribution" of the watershed parameters (Vrugt et al. 2008, https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/treatment-of-input-uncertainty-in-hydrologic-modeling-doing-hydro). These are modeling/likelihood changes (e.g., the Bayesian total error analysis of Kavetski, Kuczera & Franks 2006, https://doi.org/10.1029/2005WR004368), not FLOPs changes.
50: 
51: 2. **Intrinsic autocorrelation of a single chain.** τ is a property of target and sampler. Better samplers reduce it — adaptive Metropolis for correlated parameters (Marshall et al. 2004, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2003WR002378), differential evolution (Vrugt et al. 2009), and gradient-based Hamiltonian Monte Carlo enabled by automatic differentiation of GR4J (Krapu et al. 2022, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2021WR031377). These are the actual levers on "long chains"; hardware is not one of them.
52: 
53: 3. **Data quantity/quality.** No sampler recovers parameters the record cannot identify (Beven & Binley 1992, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hyp.3360060305; Renard et al. 2010, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2009WR008328).
54: 
55: ## 4. Synthesis
56: 
57: For the canonical problem that generates "long MCMC chains" — Bayesian calibration of a lumped conceptual model on one catchment — the binding constraint is statistical (posterior geometry, equifinality, autocorrelation, structural/input error), while the per-iteration cost is negligible. GPUs change throughput, not τ; the efficient fix is a better sampler, a reparameterization, a better integrator, or an explicit error model. So the headline answer is NOT COMPUTE-BOUND. But at two real levels — expensive distributed/high-dimensional models, and large-sample multi-catchment studies — compute is a genuine, currently-binding blocker, and there the workload is embarrassingly parallel across parameter sets, chains, and catchments, so massive GPU/cloud parallelism directly changes what can be attempted and concluded. Those are captured below as compute signals, not as the primary limiter of the "long chains" question.
58: 
59: VERDICT: NOT COMPUTE-BOUND

GPU-optimized large-basin models report ~20× CPU speedups for calibration and ~65× GPU speedups for simulations (Freitas et al. 2022, https://experts.illinois.edu/en/publications/performance-optimization-of-the-mgb-hydrological-model-for-multi-). At the SWAT end of the spectrum, calibration "could take days to complete, even on the finest standalone machines" (nhess 2012, https://nhess.copernicus.org/articles/12/2411/2012/nhess-12-2411-2012.pdf). This level is genuinely compute-bound, and parallelism is the fix because calibration decomposes into thousands of independent model runs.

Three hard limits are not computable away:

1. **Structural error and input (rainfall) uncertainty.** The model is wrong and the rainfall is mismeasured. Renard et al. 2. **Intrinsic autocorrelation of a single chain.** τ is a property of target and sampler. Better samplers reduce it — adaptive Metropolis for correlated parameters (Marshall et al. 2004, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2003WR002378), differential evolution (Vrugt et al. 2009), and gradient-based Hamiltonian Monte Carlo enabled by automatic differentiation of GR4J (Krapu et al. 2022, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2021WR031377). These are the actual levers on "long chains"; hardware is not one of them.

3. **Data quantity/quality.** No sampler recovers parameters the record cannot identify (Beven & Binley 1992, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hyp.3360060305; Renard et al. 2010, https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2009WR008328).

For the canonical problem that generates "long MCMC chains" — Bayesian calibration of a lumped conceptual model on one catchment — the binding constraint is statistical (posterior geometry, equifinality, autocorrelation, structural/input error), while the per-iteration cost is negligible. GPUs change throughput, not τ; the efficient fix is a better sampler, a reparameterization, a better integrator, or an explicit error model. So the headline answer is NOT COMPUTE-BOUND. But at two real levels — expensive distributed/high-dimensional models, and large-sample multi-catchment studies — compute is a genuine, currently-binding blocker, and there the workload is embarrassingly parallel across parameter sets, chains, and catchments, so massive GPU/cloud parallelism directly changes what can be attempted and concluded. Those are captured below as compute signals, not as the primary limiter of the "long chains" question.

VERDICT: NOT COMPUTE-BOUND

## Abstract

Recent advances in deep learning for neural networks with large numbers of parameters have been enabled by automatic differentiation, an algorithmic technique for calculating gradients of measures of model fit with respect to model parameters. Estimation of high-dimensional parameter sets is an important problem within the hydrological sciences. Here, we demonstrate the effectiveness of gradient-based estimation techniques for high-dimensional inverse estimation problems using a conceptual rainfall-runoff model. ## Model overview¶

GR4J ("Génie Rural à 4 paramètres Journalier") is a lumped, conceptual, daily rainfall-runoff model developed at INRAE (formerly Cemagref). It transforms catchment-average rainfall and potential evapotranspiration (PE) into daily streamflow using four calibrated parameters and a fixed structure of two non-linear stores and two unit hydrographs.

GR4J is widely adopted for its parsimony, computational efficiency, and good performance across a range of climates. It was developed and refined through testing on hundreds of catchments; the structure described here corresponds to the version published in Perrin et al. (2003).

...

## Calibration guidance¶

- Initial states. GR4J is sensitive to the initial values of S and R. Use a warm-up period of at least one year (longer in arid catchments) to remove their influence.
- Joint calibration. All four parameters are typically calibrated jointly because of correlations between them. X1 and X3 trade off when balancing fast and slow flow components; X2 trades off against the production store to close the water balance.
- Identifiability. X1 and X4 are usually well identified. X2 and X3 can be less well identified, especially in catchments with stable baseflow.
- Objective functions. NSE on flows emphasises high flows; NSE on log-flows or KGE-on-log emphasises low flows; KGE balances bias, correlation, and variability. Multi-objective calibration is common.

separately. The proposal distribution of each component is a 1D normal distribution, which is 
adapted in a similar manner as in the standard AM algorithm. However, the componentwise 
adaptation does not work well for distributions with a strong correlation. Safta et al. (2015)

steps of increasing dimensionality, with each intermediate step starting with an appropriate

distribution, but the computational cost used to define the proposal was rather high. 
AM is a single-chain method. With a single chain, it is particularly difficult to judge the 
convergence. Even the most powerful diagnostics, which compare the sample moments of the 
first and second half of the chain, cannot guarantee that the chain has converged to the target 
distribution (Gelman and Shirley, 2011). One solution to alleviate the problem is running 
multiple independent chains with widely dispersive starting points and then using the diagnostics 
for multi-chain schemes, such as the Rˆ statistic of Gelman and Rubin (1992), to check 
convergence. The Rˆ statistic calculates the ratio of between-chain variance to with-in chain 
variance. When the chain has a good mixing and all the chains converge to the same PPDF, the 
Rˆ value is close to one, and in practice the threshold of 1.2 is usually used for convergence 
diagnosis. On the other hand, when the chain does not mix well and different chains converge to 
the different portion of the target distribution, it is unlikely that the Rˆ will reach the value of 1.2 
required to declare convergence. Generally, this situation suggests that multiple modes exist in 
the target PPDF and the AM sampler is unable to identify all the modes using a single chain. 
2.4 DREAM algorithm 
The DREAM algorithm is a multi-chain method (Vrugt, 2016). Multi-chain approaches use 
multiple chains running in parallel for global exploration of the posterior distribution, so they 
have several desirable advantages over the single-chain methods, particularly when addressing 
complex problems involving multimodality and having a large number of parameters with strong 
correlations. In addition, the application of multiple chains allows utilizing a large variety of 
statistical measures to diagnose the convergence including the Rˆ statistic mentioned above. 
DREAM uses the Differential Evolution Markov Chain (DE-MC) algorithm (ter Braak, 
2006) as its main building block. The key feature of the DE-MC scheme is that it does not 
specify a particular distribution as the proposal, but proposes the candidate point using the 
differential evolution method based on current samples collected in the multiple chains. Thus, it 
can apply to a wide range of problems whose distribution shapes are not necessarily similar to 
the proposal distribution and it automatically chooses an appropriate scale and orientation of the 
proposal, removing the requirement of initializing the covariance matrix as in AM. As 
previously, we denote the sample at iteration t of a single chain by a d-dimensional vector xt, 
then the samples from N chains at the iteration t construct a N × d matrix saved in Xt. In DE-MC,

The DE-MC algorithm can successfully simulate the multimodal distributions, because it directly uses the current location of the multiple chains stored in X, instead of Cov(X) from a single chain, to generate candidate points, allowing the possibility of direct jumps between different modes. In addition, it has no difficulty in simulating the distributions with heavy tails, because it does not use the Gaussian proposal whose function gets small much faster than the heavy-tailed functions in the tails and thus causes sampling problems as reported in Robert and Casella (2004) and demonstrated in Section 3 of this work. The DREAM algorithm maintains the nice features of the DE-MC, but greatly accelerates the chain convergence. First, DREAM generates the candidate sample based on the difference of more than one pair of chains, which increases the diversity of the proposal and thus facilitates the updating of the proposal distribution to the target. Secondly, DREAM only updates selected dimensions when a candidate sample is generated, which improves efficiency for high dimensional problems because with increasing dimensions the performance of optimization deteriorates exponentially. What is more, the use of subspace sampling allows using fewer chains than the number of parameters, which greatly improves the computational efficiency over DE-MC that requires N=2d chains to be run in parallel. Running many parallel chains implies a potential waste of computing resources, as each individual chain requires a certain portion of

samples, which will be discarded, to get converged to the target distribution. Thirdly, DREAM 
explicitly handles and removes chains “stuck” in regions of the parameter space that are not 
contributing to the target PPDF. This strategy of handling outlier chains is very important for 
multi-chain methods, as the samples from these outlier chains will not only deteriorate the 
generation of the candidate points, which thus slow down the movement of other robust chains, 
but even worse they may prevent the convergence to the target distribution. For example, if one 
chain keeps sampling the area isolated from the target distribution that other chains are sampling, 
it will make the Rˆ statistic almost impossible to reach the threshold of 1.2 required to declare

positions of other well-performed chains, which greatly speeds up the convergence. More 
information about the DREAM algorithm was presented in Vrugt et al. (2008, 2009a, 2016) and

## Abstract

Large-scale hydrological models simulate watershed processes with applications in water resources, climate change, land use, and forecast systems. The quality of the simulations mainly depends on calibrating optimal sets of watershed parameters, a time-consuming task that highly demands computational resources from repeated simulations. 1998), whereas for distributed-memory systems the Message Passing Interface (MPI) 
is widely accepted in the parallel community (GROPP et al., 2014). Both interfaces are 
constantly employed together in a large number of applications, defining a hybrid 
approach that combines MPI and OpenMP. Moreover, high-performance applications 
can also be efficiently implemented with the Compute Unified Device Architecture 
(CUDA) developed for NVIDIA GPUs (NVIDIA, 2012). 
Furthermore, building efficient and portable applications requires additional 
performance analysis tools to guide developers on how to fully exploit the hardware 
potentials. The Cache-Aware Roofline Model (CARM) (MARQUES et al., 2020; LOPES, 
2016; ILIC et al., 2013) is a bound and bottleneck-based tool that identifies the factors 
limiting the performance (flops/s) of applications, visually representing the compute 
and memory behavior of an application/system pair, thus providing guidelines for 
optimizations according to the application’s arithmetic intensity (flops/byte). 
Given a specific computer/system, the CARM is based on defining two Cartesian axes, 
the abscissa axis with the application’s arithmetic intensity and the ordinate axis 
with the computing performance. Each application is characterized by its arithmetic 
intensity and computing performance, where either can change according to the 
degree of the optimizations. The system’s computing performance for any arithmetic 
intensity value is bound by either the memory performance (a slanted line given by 
the memory bandwith) or the computing performance (a horizontal line). Therefore, 
a 2D region is defined under these lines that resemble a roofline and each vertical 
line, which corresponds to a particular arithmetic intensity, is limited by the roofline 
to the attainable computing performance of the application. 
Applications that involve modeling the complex dynamics of hydrological processes 
require significant computational resources and are extremely important in 
environmental issues, being the subject of several recent researches that focus on 
how natural resources change in our planet. Large-scale hydrological models are 
extensively used for the understanding of watershed processes, which are closely 
connected to applications in water resources, climate change, land use, and forecast 
systems (PAIVA et al., 2011). 
Those models simulate complex nonlinear hydrological processes and usually 
contain a set of nonphysical parameters, i.e. not measurable from actual data 
2 
measured/acquired in field, which are embedded in the model to function as 
conceptual representations that express watershed characteristics, thus allowing 
the model simulated responses to satisfactorily adjust to the real-world observed data 
and simulate the behavior of the watershed (EFSTRATIADIS; KOUTSOYIANNIS, 2010), 
for instance, the watershed discharge. The calibration process is a time-consuming 
task that requires repeated model simulations, and consists in estimating the optimal 
sets of model parameters that can simulate the watershed behavior, given actual 
initial and boundary conditions. 
The estimation of the optimal sets of model parameters is solved as an inverse 
problem, which is formulated as an optimization problem iteratively solved to 
minimize specific objective functions. In this thesis, a stochastic algorithm generates 
candidate solutions that are successively evaluated by means of a multi-objective 
function, which measures, according to a norm, the difference between simulated and 
measured data. Therefore, once the sets of model parameters for a given watershed 
are estimated, the parameters can be generically used in subsequent simulations, 
providing hydrological responses of higher quality and accuracy. 
The present work targets performance optimizations on the MGB hydrological 
model (COLLISCHONN, 2001), used for simulations, and the MOCOM-UA multi 
objective calibration method, based on a double-layer approach to execute the MGB 
model at each iteration. Two watersheds were chosen for the simulation test cases, 
corresponding to the Purus (Brazil) and the Niger (Africa) rivers, but only the former 
watershed was employed for calibration. 
The MGB model implements a numerical method, referred to as inertial model, that 
solves the Saint-Venant equations to estimate water height and discharge (stream flow) 
along the longitudinal extension of the river in the watershed (FAN et al., 2014), which 
is useful to numerous hydrological applications (FAGUNDES et al., 2020; FLEISCHMANN

In the MGB model, the watershed parameters are used to set the initial and boundary

radiation, evapotranspiration, and water balance in soil. Therefore, those parameters

instead to update the variables used as input to the inertial model.

Some methods focus on only one objective function, such as the search-based and evolutionary Shuffled Complex Evolution (SCE-UA) method (DUAN et al., 1993), commonly employed using hydrological models. However, single-objective methods do not provide solutions that can truly model the behavior of the observed data in hydrological simulations, particularly in the extreme situations of wet and dry periods (TIAN et al., 2019). In contrast, multi-objective methods were developed and employed in hydrological modeling to evaluate and capture various properties of the observed data, with the critical advantage of providing hydrological models high-quality parameters that are estimated to produce more consistent and accurate simulated results (VRUGT et al., 2003), even in extreme events of floods and droughts. More specifically, the Multi-Objective Complex Evolution (MOCOM-UA) method (YAPO et al., 1998) has been successfully applied to a variety of environmental applications (FAGUNDES et al., 2019; GERITANA et al., 2014; ISLAM; DÉRY, 2017; TATSUMI, 2016; TESEMMA et al., 2015), being predominantly used for general-purpose global multi-objective optimization. In addition, an epidemic genetic algorithm (EGA) (ARAÚJO et al., 2013) was proposed as a variant of the MOCOM-UA method, to be employed in calibration using the IPH2 hydrological model developed for small basins (TUCCI, 2005). The MOCOM-UA method formulates the estimation of the sets of model parameters as an inverse problem that is implicitly solved, i.e. successively generating candidate solutions that try to minimize multiple objective functions, which express the difference between simulated and measured data. The calibration procedure is based on determinism to converge to the local/global optimal solutions (simplex search), probability to better explore the search space escaping from local minima (random search), evolution to improve the solutions (population evolution), and nonuniqueness of solutions to provide multiple optimal solutions (Pareto front). However, the optimal solutions are never assured to be found, only suboptimal solutions, as it is not possible to ensure that a given solution is optimal, specially in multi-dimensional problems. [7] Multiple-chain methods use different trajectories run ning in parallel to explore the posterior target distribution. The use of multiple chains has several desirable advantages, particularly when dealing with complex posterior distribu tions involving long tails, correlated parameters, multimo dality, and numerous local optima [Gilks et al., 1994; Liu et al., 2000; ter Braak, 2006; ter Braak and Vrugt, 2008; Vrugt et al., 2009; Craiu et al., 2009]. The use of multiple chains offers a robust protection against premature conver gence, and opens up the use of a wide array of statistical measures to test whether convergence to a limiting distribu tion has been achieved [Gelman and Rubin, 1992]. One popular multichain method that has found widespread appli cation and use in hydrology is the shuffled complex evolu tion Metropolis algorithm (SCEM-UA) [Vrugt et al. 2003]. Numerical experiments on a diverse set of mathematical test functions have shown that SCEM-UA works well in practice. Yet SCEM-UA does not generate a perfectly re versible Markov chain. The explicit removal of outlier tra jectories and covariance updating step violate detailed balance. This poses questions on whether SCEM-UA gener ates an exact sample of the posterior distribution. With some simple modifications, SCEM-UA could be made an exact sampler, but this is beyond the scope of the current pa per.
